utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, the rest of you. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Josse and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution, Mr. Mitchell, Mr. Thayer. We were informed that Mr. McCloskey won't be showing up today and tomorrow. I also have been told there are some preliminaries, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor disclosed last Friday a very large number of documents, a new series of telephone intercepts about 10.000 pages all together and 120 audio recordings, which amount to about 220 hours of recording. The Prosecutor obtained these documents last March, very exactly on March 13, 2008. I'm not -- I don't want to criticize or blame anyone for this late disclosure because I assumed that before disclosing anything, the Prosecution wanted to analyse these documents to see whether they were relevant to the case, and obviously the Prosecution needed five months to do this analysis. In March, April and May we had no hearings, however. Now Defence just got these documents and Defence has to analyse these documents itself. We analysed this last weekend, of course that was extremely brief and short, and this showed that we have documents from dating 1995, July 1995, notably documents dealing with Zepa. Of course, I'm not saying all these documents relevant to the case but in order to find the right relevant document we will have to scrutinize 10.000 pages and 120 hours of recording. I guess that if these documents had not been relevant, the Prosecution would never have disclosed it, and they did disclose it last Friday afternoon. The one Defence team has already presented its case, another Defence team is almost done with presenting its own case, so all together you could say that the Defence is in the midstream of presenting its case, so I really don't know at this stage of the proceeding what we are supposed to do. We are presenting our own case and I don't know while -- how we can analyse this amount of document while presenting our cases and while following the hearings. It's not going to be possible. We have no time, we have no resources to do this. I'm sure that no one in this courtroom needs to be reminded of Rule 25 in the Statute, according to which each accused is entitled to have enough time to prepare its own Defence. But these rights should be applied to the pretrial phase as well as to the trial phase --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: This is Article 21 of the Statute. MADAM FAUVEAU: [Interpretation] Even when you are in the middle of the trial, I believe that enough time to analyse these documents should be allocated to Defence. In order to really put my points across I would like to tell the Trial Chamber that last July 25th we also received more than 5.000 pages of documents, most of which are coming from the staff, documents bearing the signature of members of the staff. And we also had to analyse these 5.000 pages. I take this opportunity to tell you that the Defence of General Miletic was able to analyse these 5.000 pages during the summer recess but we were unable to do this because there was no hearing at the time. We are also preparing a motion in order to amend our 65 ter exhibit list. Let me reassure you there will won't be 5.000 pages, but there be quite a large amount of documents, however. All I want the to say is that we managed to go through these 5.000 documents and suddenly we are flooded with 10.000 more and 220 hours of recording. I must confess that I was quite reluctant to speak with the Trial Chamber, and in our Defence team we thought about this problem decided to address the Trial Chamber in order to protect the interest of our client. The General Miletic Defence team is absolutely convinced that the only way to protect the interest of our client was to address the Trial Chamber. I do not want to waste your time, and I thank you for your patience and for hearing me out. I'll go to the point, straight to the point. In order to analyse these new series of documents which we received last Friday, we believe that we need at least one month. We need one month. That would be a reasonable time. We are ready to make all efforts possible and try to shorten this to three weeks. But we believe that in order for at the Defence of General Miletic to prepare itself for the case afterwards we believe that once Nikolic's Defence team has presented its case and here we agree with Mr. Bourgon and Madam Nikolic but before our Defence team presents its case we believe there should be an adjournment for at least three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I just like to join to the submission of Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We join also. But I'd like to also make two additional points if we may. One related. One not directly related. I think that the late disclosure the Prosecution would have stopped giving us documents at such a late stage after the lessons we all should have learned in the Krstic case when takes were disclosed at such a late stage in the proceedings and what the Court said in that case. What respect to what Madam Fauveau said I do endorse that we get this time to review these documents. It's impossible for us to do that while being at trial and preparing our various Defence cases. Even when we are not doing the Defence cases, we are reading other accused witnesses so we can be prepared in order to cross-examine them. The second topic that is not directly related involves Witness 2DW-83. He is a DutchBat witness. I today received additional proofing or statements that that witness purportedly made to both the Royal Netherlands Army as well as to the ICTY. I just don't know why we didn't get that during the regular disclosure of DutchBat personnel and why we didn't get it when Mr. Egbers testified here many, many months ago. His name on the proofing by the investigator is attached. And although I did have a brief discussion with my learned friend I'd like to have him put on the record as to why his own investigator's information report which mentioned Egbers and this gentleman 2DW-83 was not provided to us other than this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further preliminaries? None, yes Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Let me just state Mr. Borovcanin's Defence position regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The issue that Madam Fauveau raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, we basically support Madam Fauveau's request, and we understand that this amount of disclosure which has like 220 hours, it's time consuming job to digest all this and in this sense we do support Madam Fauveau's request. However we would prefer if the Trial Chamber decides to grant Madam Fauveau's request that the recess takes place after Mr. Borovcanin Defence presents its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Just to keep the Trial Chamber informed, first of all, that we support Madam Fauveau's request for a break in the proceedings in order to review this material. However, as she did mention, the team of Drago Nikolic is ready to proceed with the Defence of our client. On Friday we disclosed a list of our witnesses that we have for September, and we are ready to proceed and at this stage we are proceeding on the assumption that we will begin as of 15 September and we could be ready to begin as early as 12 September depending of course when my colleague ends his case. That being said it is important for us to have a starting date because we are in contact with the victims and the witnesses section and it's a matter of planning as to when we will begin. All this taking into account, we still need although to review the material that was disclosed to us, that's why we support Madam Fauveau's request. At first glance it appears Drago Nikolic is not target by this new material, but we still have to review it; and it is important that we do have some kind of a recess so that we are able to review all of the new material disclosed to us. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry wait one moment. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We support Mrs. Fauveau's motion and we join in that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. President. Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll have to consult with Mr. McCloskey. I presume his absence is a pure coincidence this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has got nothing to do with Labour Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right. I can tell the Court what I know about these new intercepts which we were disclosed recently. My understanding is that these intercepts involve an entirely new site or sites of which we were not aware, did not have this material for. I don't know the ins and outs of how we actually acquired it, but my understanding is we have not even begun to analyse these intercepts ourselves. What has taken so long between the time we obtained them and the time we disclosed them is the mechanical process of miffing them and getting them into a searchable format that is intelligible to our friends; that is literally taken these several months to do. As far as I understand it, we are on an equal playing field with respect to these intercepts in terms of knowing what is in them. Our thought was just to disclose the whole lot get them to our friends as soon as we could without further delaying getting them out without going through each and every one. They are voluminous from my understanding. With respect to our friend's request, I understand that Madam Fauveau had some discussions with Mr. McCloskey, I think our position is we are not going to oppose the request outright. It may be reasonable to have to take some weeks to review these materials. As I said, we need to review them as well. They have just gotten into the system. So it will take some time. With respect to my friend's statement about the DutchBat information, Mr. Lutke was not on our initial witness list. When we run searches our all systems database searches on our witnesses before we call them we typically get binders and binders which we review when there's Rule 68 we disclose. That a wasn't done with respect to this person because he wasn't our witness. When he was placed on the Defence fence witness list that was done. Over the weekend I began reviewing the materials, I found three documents which had not been disclosed previously, I think because we probably didn't know about them when we made our initial disclosure in the course of our normal disclosure process for this witness. Again he wasn't on our witness list. With respect to why this one particular document was not disclosed in connection with Lieutenant Egbers, I don't have an answer to that. It may have not been in the binders it may have not been picked up in our prior all systems search. All I can say is that when I came across it this weekend, I immediately made hard copies of all the materials and distributed them to my friends, hopefully in time for them to be able to use them if they see fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So two things we will await further information from Mr. McCloskey to start with. Secondly, we'll back to you on Madam Fauveau's issue, matter. All right. Who is the next witness because we are were told this morning that there was some kind of decision as to whether it will be one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Bojan Subotic, Your Honour. The changes we've made this week to some of the witnesses we provided the staff with that is a result of a number of things which we are trying to accommodate everyone. The witness's schedules prior to the break had to be transferred over here, we had one who his health recently is poor. The Court was kind enough to grant the videolink we had to move him from this week the other witness for late this week at the request I think of the former accused counsel, we had to move him to next week, and it looks like we may have to move him even to the week of the 15th if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When do you reckon you will finish with your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought we'd finish no later than 12th of September, Mr. President, of September, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are move someone already to the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not, that's the points I wanted him this Friday because it fits better with what I thought was an orderly plan. Then it was requested that he move to the 8th of September and we accommodated that request because of the lawyer from America and then just this weekends we heard they can't do it the 8th but would prefer to do it the 15th. I leave it in your hands and the Prosecution, I don't know how to schedule it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can speak very briefly to that point. The request, I'm in discussions with registry to see if this is possible, the reason we are looking at the week of the 15th instead of the week of the 8th has to do with the time difference because there is a significant time difference. When we are in morning court it's impossible to set up the videolink with that particular location. So we were hoping that we would be able to schedule it for the following week when we are in afternoons. Either Monday the 15th, I understand we are in mornings typically on Mondays or Tuesday the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could also as Judge Kwon is suggesting to us get the registrar to change the sitting of the 8th from the morning to the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can flip with Gotovina that will be great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Gotovina will only be pleased to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If that can be arranged, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 8 is Monday? No, isn't it. 8 is Monday. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Okay. We'll let's leave it until after the first break and we'll tell you what our preference is and also you make your own calculations, Mr. Ostojic. All right. Mr. Subotic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are going to give evidence you have been summoned by the Beara Defence team, before you start you are required by our rules to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Text is right in front of you, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic from the Beara Defence team will go first then will be followed by others on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As you know, I'm Predrag Nikolic, I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara, and I'll be leading you on behalf of this team. Could you please first of all introduce yourself for the record.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Bojan Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your father's name, the year of birth and where you were born, please?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: My father's name is Janko. 12 of December 1972 in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, what about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I'm a welder, I completed a secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When did you complete secondary education?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And when you graduated did you work, and where you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I did not work. Six months after I completed by secondary education I joined the JNA to do my regularly military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend serving as a conscript in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: 14 and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Until what time, when were you discharged from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: From 15 March 1991, to 28 or 29 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After your compulsory military service where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I returned home and I joined the Republika Srpska army because the war in Bosnia had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What unit were you a member of in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was in the Iljas Brigade for five or six months and then in December, I joined the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the 65th Motorised Regiment, or rather from when to when?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: From December 1992 to February 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What duties did you perform in that unit?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I had several duties starting with the commander of the anti-terrorist company to the military police service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where were you, Mr. Subotic, in June and July 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was in the battalion of the military police of the 65th Motorised Regiment in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What duties did you perform there during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of the military police platoon, and I was the commander of the security of the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain, you've just told us you were also in the patrol service, what is patrol service?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The patrol service is -- encompasses different services that form the battalion of the military police that had just been established in our unit. As the word has it, this service is for patrolling and providing security for facilities, materiel, equipment, access and guards posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the time in Nova Kasaba, was it only a part of the unit that was billeted there or was there only the command of the battalion that was billeted there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The command of the military police battalion was there, but at the time there was just the command and myself providing security for the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please remember how many troops and officers of your unit were there in Nova Kasaba at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: What period are you referring it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: June and July 1995, this is the period I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: There were some dozen of us, ten or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an event that happened in July 1995 that to your mind was significant?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I remember in the first half of the month of July we were performing our regular security tasks, I was a member of the patrol together with five soldiers. When around 8 o'clock one morning a woman came that I knew by sight. She resided very close to the facilities where we were billeted; she ran up to us bare foot and she told us that her house was full of Muslims, and Muslims soldiers and that meadows and forest around her house were also full of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When that woman came up to you, what time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It was early in the morning, immediately after breakfast, around 8 o'clock in the morning. Half past 7 or 8, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And when she approached you and told you what she had seen, did you do something about that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I ordered the patrol that I commanded to be in full combat readiness. I took two soldiers with me and I also had a BOV 7 as part of my patrol detail; this is a combat vehicle of the military police. I took two soldiers to reconnoiter in the direction of the house that the woman had mentioned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you get there, to the house?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I did not manage to get there because the Zeleni Jadar river flows in front of her house, and I was ambushed. There was some Muslim soldiers with machine gun they were shooting at me from the side of her house. They opened machine gun and mortar fire in our direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I and my two soldiers returned fire, and in that situation I summoned the combat vehicle to give me machine gun support while we were pulling out of that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you try to establish where the enemy fire was coming from, and if you did, what did you find out?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The fire came from the direction of the forest looking from the house that the woman had pointed to us, and it also came from the curve of the river, from the place where the river meanders in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What prompted your decision to call for help? Why did you ask the patrol with the combat vehicle to come to your assistance?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of enemy troops there. I had my binoculars and during the 20 or 30-second break in the fire, I could see that there were up to 1.000 soldiers. There were some 50 to 70 machine guns, and we only had one round each in the rifles that we had taken with us. We only had 30 bullets and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to withdraw in the direction of your command?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, the BOV arrived and we withdrew. I was the last to get on the combat vehicle. We were under fierce fire and while we were withdrawing towards the command, I wanted to take the soldier who remained at the centre post and proceed towards military, because I realized that we could not defend the command from such a fierce attack. There was no way for us to put up resistance against such a fierce attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you receive assistance from anybody? Did you even try to get assistance?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I did try to call the command in Crna Rijeka where the 65th Regiment was. I wanted to hear their instructions. I did it over the radio, that was in the combat vehicle. However, I did not manage to get through to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long was the conflict, i.e., how long did the exchange of fire go on for?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: From our arrival and when the fire was opened until the moment we withdraw it took some 25 minutes to half an hour. So the whole situation lasted for up to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you returned in the barracks, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I refilled my clip. I took the two combat sets that we were entitled to for securing the facility. However, at the moment when we were refilling our ammunition we could hear strong mortar and machine gunfire coming from the direction of the bridge, from Koljevic Polje. Being aware of the fact that there was civilian population down there, I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, at the moment were there any other officers in the barracks but you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a Sergeant First Class Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the battalion commander, who was it, and was he there at the command at the moment?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The battalion commander was Major Zoran Malinic. He was there all the time, however; at the moment when this woman arrived and when we suffered that attack, at that particular moment, he was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you brief your commander of the situation as it was evolving around the command at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't, I couldn't. I could not get through to him at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with him at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, not at that moment, but a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After how long from your return to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Approximately two hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us the contents of your conversation? Did you brief him about the situation when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I briefed him, and I also told him that I had one wounded soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What did the commander tell you? Did he provide you with any orders or instructions?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: After I briefed him, I suggested that we pull out from there. However, he said we couldn't and that I should go on with patrolling and to replenish with ammunition since there were many civilians, women and children, in Kasaba; and we could not leave them behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you begin patrolling again, and where?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. We continued patrolling along the axis the command, then a bend on the road called "crna tacka," the black spot next to the football pitch towards Zvornik, and towards Milici, some 3 to 400 metres from our command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify something, when you say "crna tacka," black spot, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It's a traffic sign. It means it's a dangerous bend in the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As you continued patrolling, did anything happen then?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the time while we were patrolling, we sustained heavy enemy fire, but some enemy soldiers began turning themselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me how come such a situation arose that the enemy soldiers began surrendering?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: While we were patrolling and returning fire, it was a combat from the armoured vehicle, I fired six rounds of tear gas towards the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did the enemy soldiers begin emerging from that direction, from that piece of the woods?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Three or four minutes later, after the tear gas began taking effect, a group of 10 to 15 Muslim soldiers surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What did you do with the group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We disarmed them. Staff Sergeant Petrovic left with them to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where were you at the time? Did you remain in the same place or did you continue patrolling?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I stayed there for awhile. There was still combat, and we were under sniper attacks and we tried to continue with our patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, when the first group of enemy soldiers surrendered, did you interview them? Did you question them, interrogate, did you try to learn something more about the group?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked them what unit they were from, they said -- well, basically they told me that we were attacked by an entire establishment unit. I don't know where whether it is the Srebrenica brigade or regiment or something of sorts. They also said that there were many other people in the woods wanting to surrender and that there was a conflict within the group itself; some people wanted to surrender whilst others did not. Apparently there were more of those that wanted to themselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did that information assist you in undertaking any further steps?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. After I assessed the situation, I turned on the loud speaker that we had on the armoured vehicle and began asking those enemy soldiers to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did that result in any new people surrendering?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, some quarter of an hour later, a group of some 300 people surrender, around 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, in your assessment, it was a large group of about 300 people. How many of you were there in the patrol?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was there together with four soldiers, four recruit military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me a bit more in detail how the surrendering took place of that group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was at the bridge when the first group surrendered, that's when I learned that there were more people looking to surrender. And then we went further down towards the football pitch. That group surrendered vis-a-vis the pitch. There is a path there, we saw them with their arms lifted and they said, and we could clearly understand them since we speak the same language, that we shouldn't shoot them and that they were looking to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Given the size of the group that was surrendering and that there were very few of you, how did you organise that further, and where did you send the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Via the loudspeaker, I told them to throw their weapons down and that they should cross the road and move closer to the pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there any people among them who were injured?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were two seriously wounded soldiers and one that was lightly wounded. I took care of the first two. I applied some bandages, and a soldier of mine took care of the third one that was lightly wounded. I used radio communication, I contacted Petrovic to send an ambulance because there were wounded enemy soldiers. And I also expected that some combat might ensue at a later point, and I asked for reinforcements as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were those enemy soldiers doing it voluntarily, surrendering their weapons and what was their condition? Did they look tired, exhausted, or fit?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The enemy soldiers cooperated. They listened to what I was telling them, they discarded their weapons, they moved over to the pitch and they even asked me to go up to the woods with them because there were murders taking place. They said that their commanders were killing those who wanted to surrender. In any case, they begged that I should go with them up there to resolve the situation if I could. They were physically exhausted and very thirsty. Thirsty for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said you told them to go to the stadium, to the pitch; did they go there by themselves or did you provide some sort of an escort?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: They went there by themselves. We were just across the road from the stadium. I was on the armoured vehicle with the soldiers, and I was the only one who left the vehicle while my soldiers remained inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you give them water since you say they were thirsty and that that was their primary need at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Concerning the two I talked to, I gave them water while I sent the others down to the Zeleni Jadar river because we didn't have enough water for all of them, I told them to go back to the stadium after having had some water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between the river and the stadium?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: 50 to 70 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What did you do with the weapons they had discarded?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We didn't touch it. It remained where they had left it. I did not have enough people to disarm all of them in a proper way to search them for any hand grenades or anything. The weapons simply remained where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that you had another interview with a group of soldiers and that they told you that in the woods there were more people. What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I took the two I had talked to and I asked them whether they wanted to accompany me. They said they would. I took two of my soldiers while I left the other two on the road, and we went up to the woods to where they were taking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the place they wanted you to go to, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: A horrific sight. There were over 500 dead bodies. I realized that some of them had killed themselves. Some people hanged themselves, many of them were wounded. And I realized that most of those wounds were caused by explosives by hand grenades because they were irregular in shape, I realized that it must have been done by their commanders, they truly wanted to surrender themselves, and it was a really horrific sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you find any people that were still alive and did you take them prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: There was no taking any prisoners. We found five or six survivors. We aided them, we used some bandages to the extent we had any, and we took them down to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And at the stadium, the first group of prisoners was already there. By that point in time, in your view, how many prisoners were there in total?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: When I returned with the wounded, the two soldiers that remained with the armour vehicle told me that another 200 had surrendered from the other side. They came down from the other side of the forest to the part where I was. I'd say between 4 and 500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you came back from the forest, did you check whether the ambulance team had arrived since you had called for help, and what was the treatment of the prisoners that were in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Once I came back with the wounded some 10 minutes later, an ambulance team arrived, I think from the Milici hospital. They approached the prisoners and provided medical assistance, and I think two of those soldiers who had been seriously wounded were taken to the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about food, did you provide any food?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We gave them some food that we had on us, and in the barracks. It wasn't much though. At a certain point my commander appeared. Before that when I asked for an ambulance, I had told them that they should give some food as well. He then told me I should go to Milici to the bakery and shop there and take some food under the authority of the military police to take it to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to secure at least decent qualities of food given the number of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Quantities of food.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember exactly, but I think we managed to gather 100 or 150 loaves of bread from the three or four shops we gave them that and they divided it among themselves. We also had some food that had been provided for the command and the security for that day. We gave them that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Subotic, concerning the initial information that you had received from that lady in the morning. Well, by this point in time what time of day is it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please switch on the microphone to his right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around 11 or 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there any problems with the prisoners? Was there any need to introduce order?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We had no problems with them. They cooperated fully when I sent them down to the river to drink, they went there by themselves without any escort, and the same number would come back. They received the bread. I only had some problems with our civilians who came there. There were no beatings, I wouldn't have that, but there were some insults, but that was something we could not prevent from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you stay at the stadium throughout the time next to the prisoners, or did you go on with your patrolling pursuant to your commander's orders?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was there only when I brought the people in, those who had surrendered. I was patrolling all the time. I was along the river, in the forest, my radius of movement was about 500 to 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What happened next, did you undertake any measures vis-a-vis the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We didn't do anything concrete. We just disarmed them when they surrendered and we brought them to the stadium. There were even groups who went to the stadium on their own. I did not have either the manpower or the weapons to escort them at one point, I don't know how late it was, it was maybe was about 1 or half past 1 that I brought a group of prisoners who had surrendered, and I saw that there was our commander there and another member of the unit, Staff Sergeant Janusevic. And the two of them were interviewing the prisoners and taking their details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you say they were taking details, who were they taking details from, and what do you mean by "details"?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: This is in keeping with the rules of the military police service. They took details from the prisoners, the name, the name of the unit, the ID number, where they were born. Personal details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, during that period, and I'm referring to June and July, did you encounter representatives of the United Nations in your area of patrol?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I did. There were United Nations troops there. They came to our battalion command to speak to my commander on several occasions. On that same day, and I forgot to mention that, when I had that attack, there were two members of the United Nations in a vehicle which was either a PUH or something in our command. One of them during the attack on the barracks during fierce machine gunfire asked for weapons. I gave him my own rifle with three or four clip and remained with our soldier at the gate and he returned fire from my rifle in the direction of the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When the attack was over, a new group of prisoners surrendered, were the two UN soldiers still there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: They remained in the command, in the building of the battalion command. They never came down to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the stadium where the prisoners were accommodated, where was it? Could you please specify the location of the stadium with regard to the command, with regard to the road?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The stadium was on the road from military to Zvornik or to be more precise, from our command towards Zvornik on the left-hand side of the road some 800 metres from the command. Maybe 800 to 900 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During the attacks, the first one that came from the forest and the second one from the settlement, was the fire also opened on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone or switch off his microphone to his right. The interpreters are having problems hearing him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This road was constantly under fierce fire but not of the same intensity of the fire I was subject to in the morning. Still, there was mortar fire and there was also the rifle grenades being fired on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, and we are talking about sometime after noon, were there any other events, did any other officers from your command come? And if they did, who were they?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: There were our officers there, Commander Malinic, Petrovic, Janusevic and some other of our officers arrived later on, maybe two or three of them who resided close by. I suppose that commander Malinic had contacted them by telephone or otherwise, and there were also some other officer they had rang, they were recording stuff and they were carrying cameras and recorded stuff. I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What camera crews were those and when did they turn up, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I know that one was Srna, a Srna crew. Srna standing for the Serbian radio television and the others wore uniforms, and I really don't know whether they were from a unit or who they were. I wouldn't be able to tell you, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did somebody interfered with their work or were they free to record whatever they wanted to record, and what did they actually record? What did they shoot?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Nobody interfered with their work. I even received an order from Commander Malinic telling me that a team would arrive and that they shouldn't be disturbed in their work. They recorded everything. They recorded prisoners, they recorded us, and the hills from which fire was being opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did the film crews stay in that place?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Until maybe 4 or 5 o'clock in the afternoon. Until General Mladic's arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When did General Mladic appear? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: He appeared sometime in the afternoon, around 4 or half past 4 or thereabouts. I was at the stadium next to the prisoners. I happened to be there and when I turned around, I saw a PUH arriving from somewhere, and there was General Mladic with his personal security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What did General Mladic say to you or whoever was there among the officers from your unit?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was the first one to see General Mladic when I turned around. He got out of the car and asked me something to the effect of, Kid, are you alive? Where is your commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you answered?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I saluted to the general. I said I'm alive and well, and I pointed him to the commander. Actually, I went looking for the commander with the general in tow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where did all this happen? Where did you encounter General Mladic and where did you take him to see your commander?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: In the football stadium among the prisoners who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did General Mladic address the prisoners and what did he tell them on that occasion, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, he greeted them and he said, People, good afternoon, how are you. He introduced himself to them, he said I'm General Mladic, and I remember that the prisoners applauded him quite vehemently when he introduced himself. He said they shouldn't be worried it was a good thing that they surrendered he wanted to avoid any bloodshed and that they would be accommodated, fed and that they would be exchanged for some of our prisoners; but I don't remember where these prisoners were from. I don't know whether he mentioned Mount Majevica or something else. I can't remember as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a tiny correction for the transcript. I apologise it has already been corrected in the transcript. What happened next, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The general remained there maybe 15 or 20 minutes talking to the prisoners and he told them that transportation would be provided for them to go to Bratunac because in Bratunac he would hand them over to the civilian authorities who would take their names and exchange them eventually. And then he turned to me and the commander, but I am not sure to which one of us he said, I suppose it was him, he ordered us to secure the taking of the prisoners to Bratunac and that lorries and buses would be arriving in about an hour, hour and a half and he would be the one to provide their transportation for the prisoners from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he execute his order, and how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe an hour or hour 10 minutes later, the buses indeed started arriving from the direction of Zvornik and Milici and also some lorries arrived. I'd greed with the commander who had told me, Kid, I heard the general we have to do this, and I said no problem, commander. I climbed the combat vehicle and I shouted at the people that they should take a drink of water, wait for the buses and the lorries and when the vehicles arrived they should get on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And before that what happened to the sick and wounded, were they taken care of?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: All the wounded who were there were taken care of by the medical team from Milici. Another team arrived later and all the wounds were addressed and the seriously wounded were taken to the hospital in Milici. I forgot to say that before that there had been buses transporting civilians, people recognised each other, and I even allowed some of the prisoners who were recognised by their female folks to get on those buses and lorries to avoid the stadium being unnecessarily crowding up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who was on the buses? What kind of buses were those that were passing by the stadium according to you? The buses stopped, who was on those buses?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Those were civilian buses from the direction of Konjevic Polje going in the direction of Milici. They followed the civilian Muslim population, they would stop there and people on the bus us would recognise people in the stadium as their brothers, husbands and so on and so forth, and they would not proceed without them; so I was forced to allow these recognised people to get on the buses so as to enable the buses to move on. I did not want the place to become overcrowded with all these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did this happen before General Mladic's arrival or after his arrival?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can intervene a minute, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Subotic, you said that General Mladic turned to you and ordered the prisoner to be transferred to Bratunac. Where in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the elementary school there. I believe that the name of the school was Vuk Karadzic, but I'm not sure. The elementary school. And perhaps the name is Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And General Mladic also said to you that buses would be arriving in at least half an hour, and indeed the buses arrived in 10 minutes. Can I take it from your comments that it was General Mladic who arranged those buses and transportation, nobody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladic did not mention half an hour or ten minutes. He said an hour and ten minutes later the buses would arrive, and yes, he was the one who ordered us to take the prisoners to the elementary school; and he did say that he would be the one who organise the arrival of those buses. And indeed, true to his words, an hour and ten minutes later, the buses began arriving there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, is it not somewhat unusual for the superintendent commander to organise such a transportation? My question is, who actually organised those transportation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, as far as I could hear from General Mladic is what I shared with you. I don't know any of the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Subotic, how many buses were there, as well as trucks, who arrived to transport the soldiers, the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which arrived, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some six or seven buses and the same number of trucks. There was a column of about 15 vehicles in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain the trucks and buses and their size? Were these standard buses and trucks or bigger ones?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The buses were standard in size to transport passengers, they had some 50 seats, I believe. There were also some large trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were these civilian, or military vehicles, or both?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: These buses and trucks were civilian. They came without any escorts, only the drivers operated them and they had civilian registration plates. There was no military personnel on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were there and you were assigned to organise the boarding of the buses and trucks and the transport of the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: As for the transport itself, it was the drivers who were responsible for that. I was only there to organise the boarding and to see the column off to the school in Bratunac. We were there supposed to hand them over to the civilian police, to the police station there. This was particularly stressed by General Mladic when he issued that order to my commander at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What did you do in particular to get the transport going?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: At the head of the column I placed the armoured vehicle with three soldiers. I was there with them. And at the rear as additional security, a Praga was placed. We organised the boarding of the people on to the buses and trucks and the column set off around 7 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may ask for a break at this point and then resume afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You certainly may. 25 minutes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, before continuing, I'd like to go back to some of your previous answers to clarify a thing or two. Tell me this, please, how much time in total did General Mladic spend with you and your commander in front of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Around an hour or so. I can't tell you precisely. Around one hour, maybe three-quarters of an hour or full hour. Around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How much time did elapse between his departure and the arrival of the initial buses?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The same, about an hour, an hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on now. You received an order and began forming the column of vehicles. Can you explain to us how you went about it.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: At the head of the column, I placed the armoured vehicle next to the dangerous bend in the road I mentioned before. There were three soldiers and the armoured vehicle was followed by the buses and vehicles. At the rear there was a Praga with a three-strong crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How many of you military policemen and soldiers escorted the convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Eight. The armoured vehicle crew and the Praga crew, four each: Myself and three soldiers in the armoured vehicle, and the three soldiers in the Praga with their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your view, was that sufficient to provide security for the convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Definitely not, but we did not have any more personnel to do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When did you set off towards Bratunac, if you cannot tell us the exact hour, perhaps you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It was around 7, 7.30. I can't tell you any more precisely than that. Around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is the distance from the place from which you started to Bratunac in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I think some 30 to 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We arrived two hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Given the number of kilometres, did that strike you as a rather long time, and if so, why did it take you so long?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In normal conditions, it would take 15 to 20 minutes, but we were in a convoy and from the rear, from the Praga, they kept telling me that the people were demolishing the buses, breaking through windows, falling out because they were thirsty; and every now and then I would stop the convoy when I see a creek or some sort of water nearby so that people could wash themselves and drink. We stopped frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While you were stopping on the way, were there any incidents caused by the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Incidents as such there were none, but people were breaking -- smashing windows on the buses because it was so hot. They couldn't no longer stand it inside. They were thirsty and exhausted. We were stopping along the way so that they could drink some water and feel a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bratunac, who did you hand the prisoners over to, and where?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I handed them over to the members of the station of the interior in Bratunac, the civilian police. They awaited us at the entrance of the school. There was an incident there. There was a policeman who fired his rifle accidently wounding a soldier of mine and a bus driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What time of day was it when you arrived in Bratunac in relation to the time when you left Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Around quarter past 9, 9.30 in the evening. It was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about the handover process; how did that go?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was at the head of the column. I reached the gate of the elementary school courtyard. We waited there for the members of the civilian police. I came out of the armoured vehicle. One of the civilian policemen came to meet me, I told him we had POWs. He said I that he was informed of it and said that I should move the armoured vehicle so the buses could start entering the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We stayed there up to half an hour to make room for them to pass through and to dress the wounds of the soldier and driver after the incident had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were you still there as the last bus or truck entered the school compound?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. Not all of them entered the compound because there was not enough room. I simply handed them over to the policemen, we dressed their wounds. He asked me how many of them were they, I said I didn't know, and he said they would count them. And he said, Okay, you are free to go. We went back, I was at the front followed by the Praga and we went back to the Nova Kasaba command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems on your way back to Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the environs of Kravica, we were ambushed. Myself and the Praga commander, there was fire opened at us because by the time I was back at the commands, all I had left were five or six rounds. I had spent the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Judging by previous answers, it was already night. How could you then move along the road towards the command in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Before we hit the ambush, we had headlights on, but after the ambush and the exchange of fire we killed the lights, actually, we only had the so-called war lights on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the headquarters of your unit, did you report to Commander Malinic about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I did. I told him everything. I told him about the handover of the prisoners, about the ambush, and he ordered me to replenish the ammo, and to join Lieutenant Benek,who had arrived with his soldiers in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who is Lieutenant Benek, and do you know why he arrived in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Benek was the commander of a military police company, the armoured APCs company, and commander probably summoned him to join us with his unit because there were too few of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned two soldiers who were members of the UNPROFOR. What happened to them, were they still in the command when you came back that evening?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I arrived to report to the commander, I found the two of them in the commander's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, we have been discussing these important events and you said at the beginning that that was at the beginning of July. Would you be able to give us a more precise date?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: This was sometime between the 10th and the 15th of July. I know that there was a shift changeover around the 10th, and this happened maybe two or three days after the changeover of soldiers and commanders which took place on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You spent a long time with the military police battalion, you said that it was between 1992 and 1995 or even 1996. During that period of time who was the commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: During all that time, i.e., between December 1992 and January or February 1997, the commander was Major Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The battalion was on the strength of the 65th Motorised Regiment and the commander of that unit throughout all that time was Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In addition to the patrol duties, you said that you also provided security for the facility. Did you also provide security for the Main Staff during the period between 1992 and the moment you left the unit?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of our priorities. That was the raison d'etre of our battalion. Our priority was to provide security for the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. And on several occasions, I was the commander of that security for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know Colonel Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On that day, or maybe the following day, did you see Colonel Beara in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Nova Kasaba? Did you stay until the end of the month?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No. I left the next day around 3 or 4 or 5 o'clock in the afternoon. I asked the commander to grant me leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was the leave granted?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the anniversary of my brother's death, and the commander was supposed to come with me because my brother had been a member of the same battalion that I belonged to; so it would be customary for my commander to go with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was the date of the anniversary? When were you supposed to commemorate that event?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The 16th of July, that was also my brother's birthday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, you were saying that you left Nova Kasaba in the afternoon. Until then were the two UNPROFOR officers still in Nova Kasaba all the time while you were there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The two United Nations soldiers, I received an order from the commander to escort them to a place near Srebrenica, and I believe that the name of the place is Potocari. That's where their base was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Why you? Why anybody from the military police battalion if they had their vehicle, their weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: They asked to provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll stop. Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't see it leading. Go ahead, please, can you answer the question. Why were you asked to escort them when they had their own vehicle, their own weapons? You were about to start answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wanted us to provide security for them because they believed that they could not reach their base safely, and that's why they asked Major Malinic to give them escort, somebody from the patrol. And this was granted by our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So did you escort them and up to where, to which place?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. First they wanted to take their own vehicle; however, the vehicle wasn't armoured and there was still shooting going on, on the road; and that's why they decided to leave their weapons and their vehicles and get on our armoured combat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So did you drive them to their destination?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We took them to Potocari, to their base.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was that in respect of the previous event, and what was the time when you drove them there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: That was on the following day, one day after the event; and it was around 11 o'clock or maybe noon or sometime in the afternoon maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At your request, Commander Malinic allowed you to go on leave. When did you leave the unit?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I left in the afternoon because the commander told me if Lieutenant Jevdjevic did not come to take over I wouldn't be able to go; however, Lieutenant Jevdjevic turned up sometime around 1 or 2 o'clock in the afternoon and he personally drove me to Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Subotic. I have no further questions for us. Your Honours, I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no question for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did I asked for 10 minutes, but I'm believe it might take a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. No big problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: With your permission of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless it is too much longer, in which case we will intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Subotic, I'm Aleksandar Lazarevic and together with my colleagues, I represent Ljubomir Borovcanin in this case. I'm going to ask you a certain number of questions with regard to your testimony so far. These will be relatively simple questions; however if any of them are not clear to you, please tell me that and I'll rephrase. Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Subotic, what was your rank in 1994?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was a corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the same rank in 1995 or were you promoted in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: In 1995 or in 1996, I became sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In answering my learned friend's questions, you already said that in 1994 and in 1995 you were a member of the 65th Protection Regiment and that you performed different duties. Can you please tell us more specifically in 1994 in January and February what were your duties at that time, if you can remember, as a member of the 65th Regiment?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I was the warden of our internal military prison for our own members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will move very quickly through all that. Can we now see in e-court, and you will see it on your screen document number 4D00538. These are the cover pages of a file. Could you please go to the next page of this document. Mr. Subotic, you say that this document bears the stamp of the 65th motorised protection regiment in the left top corner, the date is 19 January, 1994 and you can see that this document is sent to the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska and that this document is actually a report and the duties of the officers of the 65th motorised protection regiment in the Army Republika Srpska. You can see it yourself, can't you.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you have an occasion to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't think so, but I wouldn't be sure. I have seen something similar that I was supposed to sign when I was appointed; but I don't think this was the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go to the last page of the same document, please. The page number is 05298049. This is the ERN number of the document. And at the very bottom of the document you will see that Major Milomir Savcic was the commander and that somebody signed on his behalf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was somebody who was acting on behalf of the commander when the commander was away. Who was authorised to represent the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's now pay attention to number 41 in this document you see that the person's name under 41 is Nikodin Borovcanin, sergeant by rank, who was the commander of the first squad of the technical maintenance platoon and at the same time administrator of the materiel supplies of the logistics company. Isn't that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know Mr. Nikodin Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I think so. I believe that the name does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And to your best recollection, was Mr. Nikodin Borovcanin in 1995, in July 1995, was he a member of the 65th Motorised Regiment?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And while we were still looking at the document, obviously on the 44 you can see a name by Bojan Subotic, sergeant head of detention unit of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment; can you confirm that was what is stated in this document? I apologise, you will have to speak out and say your answer into the microphone, so it may be recorded.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at another document, 4D00539 is the number of that document. It seems that this document has not been put on e-court yet. I will, therefore, provide you with a hard copy of the document, and the copies of it have already been distributed amongst other participants in the proceedings. Just for the record, this is a logbook of daily orders of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and the page that you have before you bears the ERN number 06276263. [In English] I apologise for the transcript, on page 42 line 9 [sic] it says 65th motorised, it says here the detection regiment but it's protection regiment. [Interpretation] Maybe we could place a copy of the document on the ELMO, if I could ask for the usher's assistance. Well, it seems that it is in e-court after all. No, it is not. Yes. [In English] Maybe for the benefit of the accused, the B/C/S version should be put on the ELMO. [Interpretation] Mr. Subotic, let's look at the daily order. On the left-hand side of this document, and you will see that the date is the 10th of July 1995, and under item 1 entitled "On Duty Service" the names mentioned are Nikodin Borovcanin and his assistant soldier Jugoslav, Dzambas, can see that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And they have been appointed as officers on duty for the 11th of July 1995 as well pursuant to this daily order, wouldn't that be the case?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until sometime around 8 or 9 o'clock in the morning, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well performing the duties, the persons who are appointed as duty officers, do they have access to the means of communication with other units?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the other units of the regiment or all the other units of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Both, the regiment and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Only with some of the units of the regiment. As for the rest, they would not be able to communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question, if you know, of course, in addition to Mr. Nikodin Borovcanin were there any other persons sharing the same family name in the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and I'm not only referring to the officers, but also the foot soldiers, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes there were. I remember both soldiers and civilians serving in the army. They were mostly serving in the logistics units either as cooks, drivers and so on and so forth. That's when it comes specifically to the 65th regiment, I can't remember their first names; but there were some people sharing the same family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, we will no longer need this document. Now, I would like to move on to another topic. In the course of your testimony you have spoken about General Mladic arriving in Nova Kasaba and delivering a speech in the stadium and then after that buses started arriving. If I understand you well, General Mladic was the one who issued the order for the transport to be organised from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac, wouldn't that be correct.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. And when it came to escorting prisoners of war, he was the one who issued the order, and as far as I could understand, he was the one to issue all the other orders for the transport to be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And was General Mladic the one that said that the prisoners should be transported to the school, Vuk Karadzic, in Bratunac and nowhere else?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And General Mladic was also the one who told you to hand them over to the civilian police in Bratunac, that was also General Mladic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. My commander asked him specifically who should all those people be handed over to, and he answered everything will be organised, you will hand them over to the public security station in Bratunac, to the police in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, I paid attention to one little detail. You said that the prisoners had been listed, their names were taken, those that were in Nova Kasaba, was actually a list made of all their names, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I could notice, as I was returning with a group of prisoners, I found the Staff-sergeant Janusevic taking their details according to the rules of the military police.
