As far as I remember, some lists had been drafted, but I don't know to they were handed over to. I don't know what happened to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise we have to wait and make a short breaks to allow for the answers to be recorded. If I understand you well, you were the one who organised security for the convoy.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Major Malinic, my commander, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And in escorting the convoy, you were the officer with the highest rank, the rest were foot soldiers, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the highest ranking officer on the BOV. And the commander of Praga who had a higher rank but he was not a member of the military police. He was an artilleryman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So the Praga was not on the strength of the 65th Protection Regiment was it?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, you are wrong, the Praga was on the strength of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I misunderstood your answer. In any case, from your previous answer I understand that you did not have any lists on you, no lists of prisoners when you set off from Kasaba and headed towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I remember that I had specifically asked the commander to provide me with those lists, but the commander replied that he would send the list officially by official channels to the police over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you told that the prisoners were supposed to be handed over to the military police as a matter of fact, the military police of the Bratunac Brigade when you arrived at the Bratunac school? Was that something that was ordered to you, something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, I heard General Mladic's orders loud and clear and Commander Malinic was also there, and he can confirm my words. General Mladic specifically ordered us to hand over the prisoners to the police, and the police was waiting for us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You've already spoken about that, but let me just clarify something. At that moment your commander was Lieutenant Colonel Milomir Savcic, can you confirm that at the time of these events, this was indeed the case?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think it was the lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In any case, Milomir Savcic was the commander of the 65th mechanized Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Savcic provided a statement to the Prosecutor's Office of The Hague Tribunal on the 17th October 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have in e-court document 1D00196, page 57 in the B/C/S and 37 in the English version. Sir, on your right-hand side you see page 57 of the statement provided by General Savcic to the Prosecutors of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To the investigators, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please focus on the following sentence, it is on the bottom half of the page beginning with "yes, yes, yes." Can you read out what it says?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The left side or the right side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The right side. Start from -- can you see that there is a question just before that and there's an answer which says there were some military policemen there escorting the convoy which means that Mladic came with the buses, trucks and other stuff.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Can I read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to do that, you can read it for yourself. Did you manage to read the whole paragraph that begins with "yes, yes, yes." It is clear in the paragraph that the prisoners were handed over to the military police of Bratunac Brigade and that they had geographical jurisdiction. This is what Savcic said to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I can see that, but I know who I handed them over to. I remember the incident when the policeman wounded soldier of mine and a driver. It was the policeman who took over the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Therefore you stand by what you said today?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I listened to your testimony today and since that Colonel Beara's Defence provided us with some proofing notes for your testimony. I noticed something there that you didn't say today. I just wanted to put it to you. At that time during the proofing you told Colonel Beara's Defence that you handed the prisoners over to a civilian police who held the rank of lieutenant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: He did not sport any rank, but that's how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but he surely didn't tell you, I am a lieutenant; did he also share his first and last name with you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, his last name, but I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You can remember neither the first nor the last name of the person?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I cannot, that was the first and the last time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe him for us, as best you can remember, his height, age?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: He was rather tall, heavily built, dark hair. He was a bulky man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What about the uniform he wore, could you describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: He had a blue camouflage uniform worn by the police in towns and settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What about the other two policemen, you said that he was there plus another two policemen, did they have the same uniform or different ones?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The ones who waited there with their official vehicle had the same uniforms. Around the school, there were other policemen wearing the same uniforms. There were also many civilians wearing parts of the military uniform just a pair of pants or a shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What about the uniform, did it consist of only one or several parts, of course I mean the police uniforms we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I think they were made of two parts. They had blue police vests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What about any insignia?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It only said "police."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You said you did not see what the rank of the policeman was but that he introduced himself as a lieutenant; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, if you were to tell you that in July 1995 in the police of Republika Srpska there were no ranks at all and that they were introduced only as of November that year, would that mean anything to you concerning your testimony? Do you still stand by what you said?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I am familiar with that fact. Before that time they did have ranks, and they went by those ranks. I don't know whether he lied to me or not. He said I'm a lieutenant of the Bratunac police by a particular last name that I cannot recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Subotic, before this Tribunal there was testimony that it was the military police of the Bratunac brigade that was securing the prisoners in the Vuk Stefanovic Karadzic school in Bratunac. In order to be able to support that, I'd like to direct your attention to a certain pages of transcript of the 9th of November 2006, pages 3805, 3806, and 3909. Then in the Blagojevic, Jokic case pages 5732 and 5733. Such testimony came directly from members of the military police of the Bratunac brigade as well as from officers of the Bratunac brigade. They all said it was the military police of the Bratunac brigade that was securing the Vuk Karadzic school. Having in mind everything I've just said, do you still stand by what you've said, i.e., that it was the civilian police that was securing the school?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was securing the school, and at what time. What I do know is who it was that I handed the POWs to. It is possible that the military police was providing security for some facilities including the school, I don't know what their authority was, but I handed over the POWs to the civilian police to a patrol with an official vehicle which had rotation lights on because by that time it was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Subotic. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone. We cannot hear the counsel, he needs to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, we didn't receive ... [Microphone not activated] what was happening the reason is that it is you are too far from the microphone the interpreters couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will change the position. Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is not the microphone it is the fact that Mr. Krgovic should speak into the microphone. He is too far from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I would suggest that you switch on the other one. Keep it as high as possible because that seems to be the problem. You are too tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to come closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Subotic, during your testimony, my learned friend, Mr. Nikolic, asked you about the date when the events you've been describing took place. You said that it was two or three days after the shift, the rotation of the shift. It is evident before this Tribunal that those events took place on the 13th of July 1995, would you accept that as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your answers you've been talking about certain measures you took. Before you encountered the 28th column on that morning the 13th of July 1995, did you or commander receive a specific order that would have to do with a passage of the Muslim column or did you react spontaneously as a result of the fact that the column simply showed up?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We had received no orders, at least I didn't. I can't tell but commander Malinic. But in any case, he never told me that I should strengthen the patrol. We reacted spontaneously. There was a shift change and people went home. Had anything been planned, I believe the people would not have been allowed to go home. There would not have been any shift change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July you and your commander as far as you can tell, received no specific orders from your superior commands concerning the way you should conduct yourselves and in that situation?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, at least I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Until what time did most of the Muslim shoulders remain at the Nova Kasaba stadium? You said that by noon there were 4 to 500, and then some others came. Until what time were they at the stadium in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Until we formed the column to Bratunac, that's where they were taken. I'd say, 7, 7.30 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And by that time you were not informed by your commander of the existence of any particular orders that would have to do with the passage of the Muslim column?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, there was no specific order. We were both there at the stadium and the command truth be said, we didn't know what was going on. It was the prisoners who told us that they belonged to a brigade or a division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, during that period did you establish a checkpoint in order to control the road between Zvornik and Bratunac in Nova Kasaba? Did you maintain control of that road?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was one of the duties of my regular patrol to control the traffic, and we were supposed to do that together with the Milici police station; but on that morning I did send out a soldier who used to be at the gate as a duty soldier to the road to control the traffic and to tell people that they shouldn't use the road since they could be opened fire at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose you were informed of all persons who on that day passed by arriving in Nova Kasaba and saw and had access to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to the military police, the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The military and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Subotic, do you know General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that day in Nova Kasaba when the journalists, came, the teams of journalists, did you see General Gvero among them?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And save for General Mladic whom you saw, there were no other high ranking officers in Nova Kasaba on that day, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, you described the regular duties of your patrol, the military police. In addition to that did you ever escort officers from the Main Staff who would go to the frontline or to the meetings that were connected with a high level of risk?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was our specialty as part of our anti-terrorist training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As you performed those duties, did you ever escort General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose before the events that were -- took place in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how did you go, did you go in the same car or did you travel in a separate car behind the general or in front of him?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We shared the same vehicle. We travelled together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific trip that took place between April and June 1995? Did you escort General Gvero anywhere that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I believe that I escorted him to Banja Luka to an assembly meeting. I believe that there had been some threats against the general on the part of Karadzic, I believe or somebody like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the vehicle that you travelled in on that occasion? Do you remember the make or the colour or both?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It was a green car and it was either an Opal or a Renault. In any case it was a greenish colour I can't remember the make exactly but it was either an Opal or a Renault.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see General Gvero travelling in a black car?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Subotic, I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Mitchell I'm going to ask you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution about your testimony today. I'd like to start off just asking you a couple of questions about the structure of the 65th Protection Regiment. You've told us that in July 1995, the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment was Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic; correct.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the commander of the military police battalion was Major Zoran Malinic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And his nickname was "Zoka"; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, the deputy commander of the military police battalion, that was Alexander Lucic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the commander of the first military police company was Marinko Jevdzevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Marinko Jevdzevic was the commander of the anti-terrorist company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Jevdzevic returned Nova Kasaba from Sarajevo on 14 July; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, one day after the event he arrived and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But on the day of the fighting, on the 13th, the other officers Major Malinic, Aleksander Lucic, they were in the Nova Kasaba area?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I remember that Malinic was there, but I don't know about Lucic. I can't remember. It's possible that he was there. Usually the commander and his deputy are not in the same place. One is normally on leave, but it is possible that he was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to just take you very quickly to, can I have 65 ter number 3621. Page 12 in the English and page 11 in the B/C/S. So this is an interview with Zoran Malinic from December 2005. I just want to read you little bit of it. He is talking about the 12th of July when he received information from General Zivanovic about the column arriving and he says he is talking about the measures he can take with the number of soldier that is he had. He says: "I think that cure during that evening we called senior officers and soldiers that were sent home earlier. Any soldier that was actually still close to where we were. I remember two senior officers, one of them was my deputy, he had already gone on leave. And he wasn't there on the 12th, so he returned back on the 12th so that he could be with us." So Zoran Malinic, he is saying that Alexander Lucic returned back on the 12th of July to be with the unit in Nova Kasaba; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It is possible that he returned on the 13th, on the 12th he was on leave. I know that the commander and his deputy are not in the same place at the same time, but anything is possible. I'm not sure about the 12th, but I'm sure that he was there or I seem to remember that he was there on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, so what was your rank in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And how many men were there in your unit?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And did you receive reinforcements during the day on the 13th when all the fighting was happening?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening Lieutenant Benek arrived with two APCs and some 30 men or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But during the day, it was you and your six men?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had six men. However, on that particular day, I only had five because one soldier was on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you were running short on ammunition as well?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that you and five soldiers with limited ammunition arrested hundreds and hundreds of Muslim men along the road in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We did not arrest them. They surrendered to us. There is a big difference between arrest and surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, so you told us that the road was under fire all day; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But despite being under fire and you having very limited resources, you told us that you took two soldiers and went into the woods because you were told that there were more Muslims there; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: There is no reason not to believe 200 or 300 men who were telling me the same story. I knew where they were coming from, and there was no reason for me not to believe what side they were on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So on the 28th of August this year, we received a copy of a statement that you gave to the Beara Defence; and I'd just like to read back a little bit of that statement to you, if I can. Can I put a copy on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a statement but a proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, I'll just read back what you said to the Beara Defence team. They said: "The witness bought several of the prisoners to show him where the rest of the Muslim soldiers are, and then he came to the place where many dead Muslims killed in the fighting amongst themselves as well as one Muslim who was hanged." Now, sir, in your statement you said that there were many dead Muslims killed in the fighting; correct? Killed in the fighting among themselves.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: When I took the two Muslim prisoners to where they led me, I realized that the 500 dead bodies were the result of their in-fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's what I'm interested in, sir. You told the Beara Defence team that there were many dead Muslims killed in the fighting, and today we hear 500 bodies. Did you tell the Beara Defence team that there were 500 bodies?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember the details of our conversation, but I remember well that in two or three place that I inspected, there were around 500 bodies as a result of suicide, shots in the head, irregular wounds as a result of hand grenade suicides; and I still remember the picture of that young man who had hung himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's the next thing I'd like to ask you about. In your statement you said that there was one Muslim who was hanged, and yet today you testified that some people hanged themselves. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: First of all, I never provided any statements to anybody. I did talk to the Defence, but I did not make any notes. Maybe they did not reconstruct properly what I told them. I remember that I told them that I saw one person who had hanged himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, you testified earlier today that you placed your Praga and its crew at the dangerous bend in the road near Nova Kasaba; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I suppose I remember. I only mentioned Praga as the vehicle at the back of the convoy of prisoners when we escorted them to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can just have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move to a different area now, and ask you some questions about the prisoners who were at the Nova Kasaba stadium on 13 July. You testified that when you first came to the stadium there were around 500 prisoners there; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No. When I first arrived at the stadium there was nobody there. That was very early in the morning. The first group consisting of some 15 members surrendered, and then another group of some 2 to 300 of their members surrendered to me personally; and then I took that second group to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So this is later in the morning that there's 500 men at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Around noon or maybe 1300 hours, it was at that time that there were about 500 people in the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, we have evidence in this case that by 1400 hours there were over 1.000 prisoners being held at the Nova Kasaba stadium. Does that help you remember when you saw 500 men at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there were 1400 men. As far as I can remember, the total number was around 1.000 or 1200 at the most. 1400 seems like a lot, and as for the 500 that I saw, it was around 12 or maybe half past 12 or 1300 hours. I wouldn't be sure. And it's really not a very easy thing to be very specific about, time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So just to summarize, sir, on the 13th of July you spent sometime at the stadium in Nova Kasaba, you spent a lot of time patrolling the road, at one point you went down to Milici to get bread, and later on in the afternoon you led the convoy buses to Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that you moved around a lot on that day, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I've just a couple of questions about a different area. Sir, you told us that you saw two UN soldiers at your command in the morning; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you only see two soldiers or did you see any other UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: That morning there were two, and the day before I believe a day or maybe two days before there were several UN soldiers, they came to and fro; they looked for some security as far as I can remember. But on that particular day there were only two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, at any point during that day did you see any UN soldiers being placed on top of a UN APC or a BOV where there were Serb soldiers inside that APC or BOV?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I did see their vehicles. I don't know what kind of vehicles those were, but I did not see our troops in any of them. When I say our troop, I mean the troops of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You didn't see any VRS soldiers in the UN vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: At any point did you see any Serb forces, any Serb soldiers wearing or using United Nations equipment?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: You mean on that day or in more general terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: On that day?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think it might be time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25 minute --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me? Sorry, Mr. President, if we could just have an indication of the time because I think the next witness is here, should we keep him, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. Ostojic. Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Less than half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding we have approximately 10 to 15 minutes, it still depends on the other questions but just so the Court is aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean you have 10 to 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Redirect. We'll finish with this witness today for sure, and we can send the other witness home or not home, I don't want to be misinterpreted. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you know where your Praga was on 13 July before you placed it at the back of the convoy that went to Bratunac? Do you know where it was positioned?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: In the courtyard of the school where our command was. It was providing security for the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you know if it was firing at Muslim positions?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It fired on one or two occasions. I think the first time was facing the house from which the woman had come, but I think that was the only occasion when it was discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So it wasn't firing into the woods at any point?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, it did fire on a couple of occasions in the direction of the house, but the house is just before the forest. It is very close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go back quickly to something you said just before the break. Now, you drew a distinction between whether these men were arrested or whether they surrendered. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: is it your testimony that hundreds and hundreds of armed Muslims were killing themselves in the forest and hundreds more were surrendering to you and your five men, but there was only you and your five men on that stretch of the road, your Praga wasn't even deployed on that stretch of the road?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It only went as far as the bridge in our direction, and it was some 200 metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, my question was, is it your testimony that hundreds of Muslims were killing themselves and surrendering, but there was only you and your five men there? It was you and your five men against hundreds of armed Muslims, and yet they were surrendering to you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Save for myself and five of my men, our commander was there with another two or three officers from our MP battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Which officers were there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Major Malinic, Sergeant First Class Kunusevic [phoen] Staff Sergeant Petrovic, well they are NCOs; and there may have been Captain Lucic, I think he was there, but I'm not absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified that back at the stadium about 4 p.m. General Mladic arrived and gave a speech to the prisoners. Now, you saw General Mladic give this speech; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't a speech as such, but he talked to the men. I saw him do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And was Major Malinic there as well?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you about an incident that happened during General Mladic's speech. And if I can have 65 ter number 2207. It's page 10 in the English. Sir, this is the statement of a Bosnian Muslim man who testified that he was captured near Nova Kasaba on 13 July. He was taken to the stadium in Nova Kasaba, transported to Bratunac and then ultimately to the Branjevo farm where he survived the execution of over 1.000 Bosnian men. Now, he says in his testimony he talked about General Mladic's speech and then he says: "Then he ordered the soldiers to make a list of the names of those captured. At that moment, a prisoner got up and the Serb soldiers approached. They kicked him and hit him with their rifle butts and then one soldier took out his pistol and killed him. And he was thrown into the other. Mladic was present, he didn't respond in any way." Sir, you remember General Mladic's speech and you were there, do you also remember this man being killed in front of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I claim full responsibility that no one was killed in the presence of General Mladic. There were no incidents of that sort whatsoever. I remember this speech, and I remember General Mladic strictly ordering us not to beat or kill the prisoners; but to treat them in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, they were many, had they not cooperated with us, me and my men would not have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. On the Exhibit 65 ter number 2207 at page 64 line 4 my learned friend says page 10, the actual transcript starts with this at 3015, so he could just give me an accurate page, so I could follow along I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Page 10 in e-court. Sorry, it's transcript page 3024.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that later in the day you organised the security for the convoy of buses and trucks that went to Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you were ordered to go to the Vuk Karadzic school; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, as ordered by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you have any communications equipment with you when you were escorting the convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had radios, GP 200 the plain police Motorolas, and we had our regular devices in both the armoured vehicle and the Praga.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you told us that there were six or seven buses in the convoy; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It is six or seven, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And these buses hold approximately 75 men each; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: There may have been more. There are I think 75 seats but perhaps a bus like that could hold up to 90 or 100 because some of them can stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your testimony that there were between 90 and 100 men on each of these buses?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Around 90, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And there were also six or seven trucks in the convoy, you said?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And how many men were there in each truck?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. We didn't count. Maybe 50 or 70. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And were all the men transported in one convoy or was there another one that left either before or after you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: At that moment there were those in the stadium and the group of the 15 prisoners which took prisoner first, they also went to the stadium to join the convoy. We transported all of them to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So all of them went in your convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has seen a lot of evidence in this case that Muslim men were surrendering to the Serb forces all day along the Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, Bratunac road just as the same they had in Nova Kasaba. You must have seen that in your trip to Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: In certain places I could only see our soldiers and policemen. As for any specific prisoners, no. Anyway, by that time it was getting dark but I can tell you that there were no crowds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We've heard a lot of evidence from both Serbs and Muslims about a large gathering of prisoners on a meadow beside the road in Sandici, which is on the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac. There were several hundred to 1.000 men who were detained there during the afternoon of 13 July. You don't remember seeing anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know where Sandici is. I was securing the convoy and the five or six metres around it, meaning the road, the transport; that was my extent of my activity and orders. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sandici is on the road between Konjevic Polje and Kravica, and the prisoners were detained in a meadow right next to the road. You didn't see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not; I had a lot on my mind. When the column would stop, sometimes I had to go to the rear to radio someone. I was either at the front or at the rear with the Praga depending on the prisoners' requests for water. That's what preoccupied all of my attention. As for the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Who did you talk to on the radio while you were leading the convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I talked to the Praga crew commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I just clarify that with you. You just told us that you sometimes had to go to the rear to radio someone. Wasn't the Praga at the rear?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't go all the way to the rear to radio anyone, but to help the rear to secure passage and provide safety for the prisoners who were leaving the buses so that there would be no clashes between them and any of the soldiers or civilians who began gathering by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And this was when you were stopping along the road and the prisoners were getting out and going and having a drink at the river; right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has also heard a lot of evidence that later that day those prisoners who were at Sandici were taken down the road to the agricultural warehouse in Kravica and executed towards the end of that day and into the night. You were ambushed at Kravica on the way back so you must know where Kravica is; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I do more or less where Kravica is, at least the centre of the village. I was ambushed as you enter Kravica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you know where the agricultural warehouse is, right next to the road?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you see any executions when you drove past that warehouse? Do you remember seeing anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You didn't see any bodies outside the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No. If the warehouse is the place that I'm thinking of, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you see any Serb forces there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I saw forces along the way from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac, but not many of them. Perhaps two or three at a time, and then I would see another group a couple of hundred metres further down the road. This resembled patrols of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But you didn't see any particular concentration of them at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No. The only concentration was that of the civilian police in Bratunac around the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you here any shooting around the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: In a distance, up in the hills, in the forest occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And how about on your way back from Bratunac, did you notice anything unusual at the warehouse? Anything at all?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I was ambushed before the warehouse, if that's the building I have in mind. I ordered my soldiers to turn off our lights, to turn on our war lights. We were short of ammunition, and we kept on pressing for the command because we could not engage in combat any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you saw nothing unusual at the warehouse on your way home back to Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I couldn't even see the road then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you just remind us what time did you arrive in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Around 9.30 in the evening, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And we've heard you talk about the police to whom you handed over the prisoners. Other than these three policemen, what other Serb forces were there guarding the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I saw another police vehicle with two members in it, in the school compound. I don't know, I couldn't see because I didn't go there. Around the buses and trucks when I arrived, there was only a large number of Serb civilians without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You were telling us that this school with hundreds of prisoners and buses and vehicles with additional prisoners was secured by three civilian police officers and Serb civilians without weapons, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether any of the prisoners were in the school. I didn't go in. All I can tell you is about my prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You handed your prisoners over to three civilian policemen, that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I handed them over to a member of the police who introduced himself as a police officer. He asked me how many were there, I couldn't tell him and he said, Well, no matter, we'll count them. I asked him if I was free to go and he said, Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, what was your understanding of what would happen to these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: To be honest in listening to General Mladic's words, I believed what he told them. However, later on in the media I heard of things. I don't know whether they are true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I heard in the media that there were murders around Zvornik or Pilica; I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The first time that you learned that the prisoners that were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school were executed, the first time you heard that was in the media?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, since I went home the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did the buses that you took the prisoners in from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac, did those buses stay in Bratunac when you left?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did the buses stay at the school or did any of them go over to the football stadium at Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just to go back for a second, these reports that you said you heard in the media, when did you hear these reports?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: After some 15, 20 days ago -- after that and perhaps a month later. Since I lived in Sarajevo, I could hear it on both the Bosnian and Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you see any other buses in Bratunac with prisoners on board?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So I have one final area I'd like to ask you about. Now, you know as well as anyone that the column of Muslim men who you engaged with on the 13th of July presented a grave risk to the Serb territory it was travelling through; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what risk they were. I only know that I was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: On 13 and 14 July, and particularly 15 and 16 July around Baljkovica the Serb forces were heavily engaged in fighting that Muslim column; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. On the 16th of July, I was at the cemetery commemorating my late brother's death in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You don't know about the fighting around Baljkovica on the 15th and 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you know that during that same period Serb forces were also tasked to sweep the terrain around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I was on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And are you aware that Serb forces from the Zvornik brigade, the Bratunac brigade, and the 65th protection regiment among others were engaged in the operation against Zepa during this period?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I said I really don't know where my unit was. I was on leave and my leave was for some seven or eight days. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, we know that the threat to Zvornik was so great that the VRS pulled troops out from around Zepa and sent them back to Zvornik. We also know that there was talk of mobilising civilians, we know soldiers were sent from the Krajina corps and MUP forces were sent from all over Bosnia. We also heard earlier that Zoran Malinic ordered his officers to return on the 12th, that is Aleksandar Lucic was ordered to return. It's your testimony that in the midst of everything that was going on that you were given a week's leave starting from the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm a technician. I'm not a strategist, I really don't know what the command and the police did at the very top. And as far as my leave is concerned, this had been arranged before because my brother was a member of the battalion of the military police the same that I was, and the commander and two more men were supposed to go as well because that is a custom in our parts. However, because of the events, they couldn't go, and I was the only one who was allowed to go on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: May I just have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, please try to conclude by quarter to 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Subotic, let's just clarify some terms here. When I examined you, you said that on the way back from Kravica after the ambush you returned to your command under war lights. Can you please explain the notion of war lights, what is that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: These are greenish lights, very small lights whose beam cannot be more than half a metre to a metre in front of the vehicle. Not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Borovcanin's Defence team examined you, you were confronted with General Savcic's statement provided to the OTP and in his statement General Savcic stated that the prisoners that you had escorted were handed over to the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know that General Savcic testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To be very objective I would like to say that it was on the 12th of September 2007, that when he testified under the same oath as you are today.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On that occasion General Savcic on page 15292, line 1, was asked about the surrender of the prisoners and he stated that he remembered the event and I quote: "But currently I don't have the transcript in front of me. If I said I had been hand over to the military police over the Bratunac brigade then I misspoke." Are you aware of that, are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I said I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the same page, line 21, General Savcic stated, "Yes, I can see that but I have to correct myself." Mr. Subotic, you handed the prisoners over or rather escorted the prisoners from Bratunac -- to the Bratunac school, could you please repeat for the Trial Chamber who you handed them over to?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I handed them over to the civilian police, to the public security station in Bratunac. At least that was what the person who was in charge introduced himself to me, he said that he was in Bratunac. He said that he was a lieutenant, and he was equipped as a policeman would be. He wore a uniform and had all the other things that would be worn by a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To my learned friend's question you described the policeman's uniform. Are you a hundred percent sure that that was indeed what he wore?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, in your unit were there any other persons who shared the same first name "Zoran"?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Name one?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know there was a Lieutenant Zoran Benek, who was the commander of the military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname of any kind?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I can't remember. We all had nickname that is we used in our mutual communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Documents? Mr. Nikolic, do you have any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic? You've got two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we already submitted ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 538 and 539. Any objections Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And any objection from the other Defence teams? None. So they are all they are both admitted. Do you have any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No documents. Thank you. Mr. Subotic, we've come to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to that you so much for coming here to give testimony and on behalf of everyone I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Incidentally before we adjourn, in relation to the previous Witness Kerkez, we admitted those photos in evidence as exhibits. Did you have any other documents that you wished to tender, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We did not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same applies to you Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. So madam registrar and ourselves have been actively working on a plan to accommodate the two video conferences, videolinks, sorry, that are in the pipeline. We are still awaiting a confirmation that other Chambers are prepared to accommodate our needs as well, so I can't guarantee that because obviously everyone has its own requirements. But if it works out, then we will have Jovanovic or whatever his name is on the 9th in the morning, and then the other videolink connection if we manage to swap our sitting from the morning to the afternoon, it will be on the 10th and the 11th. The understanding would be the following: That having looked at the time estimates, you will need to finish with Jovanovic in one day, that's on the 9th, which is within the time estimates. And the other guy on the 10th and the 11th, that is two days. And that again is within the estimates of six hours 45 minutes or something like that. So that's the understanding. But we will communicate to you a confirmation of this arrangement tomorrow hopefully when we have confirmation from the other Chambers. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
